## Where This Fits
This week comes before the architecture weeks because the tokenizer is **the design decision that is most expensive to correct after training**. Once the vocabulary is fixed, the embedding and unembedding matrices — and every FLOP already spent on pre-training — are tied to it. It is not impossible to change (vocabulary extension with continued pre-training, and tokenizer transfer, both exist), but every route back means paying for training again, with no guarantee on the result. Its downstream effects are also larger than the word "preprocessing" suggests: vocabulary size is now a variable in scaling laws, and a 2026 preprint argues that a tokenizer's compression rate shifts the compute-optimal parameter/data allocation. For a class taught in Traditional Chinese this week carries extra weight: differences in token fertility translate directly into cost and into effective context length, and some of the most frequent characters of Taiwanese and Hakka fall outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, where the price is higher still. This is also the first component in the course that we build from scratch — written live in class; the code and the reference implementation are in the *Demos* section below.

## Learning Objectives
1. **Compute by hand** the merge sequence of BPE on a small corpus and the encoding it produces, read a reference implementation, and state how BPE, WordPiece (likelihood-based merges) and Unigram LM (top-down pruning) differ in **what they optimize**.
2. Draw the four-stage tokenizer pipeline (normalization → pre-tokenization → subword model → post-processing) and say which stage determines the behaviour of digits, whitespace and special tokens.
3. Distinguish **byte-level BPE** from **byte fallback** as two mechanisms for eliminating out-of-vocabulary characters, and use UTF-8 byte counts to explain the fertility cost each imposes on CJK, including characters in the supplementary planes.
4. Explain why vocabulary size enters the scaling law, give the intuitive argument that larger models deserve larger vocabularies, and enter the tokenizer into the compute ledger: embedding parameters, the unit of $D$, and inference cost per byte.
5. Diagnose at least four downstream failures caused directly by tokenization (multi-digit arithmetic, character-level tasks, glitch tokens, unequal cost across languages, the prompt boundary) and, for each, state the strength of the evidence: which are mechanistic, which are only correlational.
6. Compare the three routes available when a language is short-changed by a tokenizer — vocabulary extension, tokenizer transfer, dropping the tokenizer — and the price each one pays.

## Demos
Three programs are run live in class this week. **You are not required to run anything** — the numbers on the slides are the rehearsal records checked in with the code — but the code is published so that you can read it, re-run it, and change it. Each folder's `README.md` gives requirements, setup, commands, and what you should see; the index at [`demos/`](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos) explains the shared environment.

| | Slide | What it shows | Needs | Runs on |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Demo 1 · one set of texts, nine tokenizers](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w02_d1_fertility) | p10 | Eight texts (a Traditional Chinese paragraph, its English and Simplified versions, Taiwanese in Han characters, a Tâi-lô sentence in NFC and NFD, a Hakka sentence with 𠊎, eight lines of Python, two numbers) through GPT-2, o200k, Llama 3, Qwen3.8, Gemma 4, Mistral, Breeze, bert-base-chinese and ByT5: token counts, tokens per character, bytes per token, the painted segmentation, the cross-language cost, and the embedding share of a real `config.json` | `transformers` (tokenizers only), `tiktoken`, `opencc`; a few MB of tokenizer files | any laptop, CPU, seconds |
| [Demo 2 · BPE by hand: one loop, one changed line](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w02_d2_bpe) | p26 | A complete BPE trainer / encoder / decoder in plain Python on the five-word toy corpus of the slides; `get_pairs` is written live, the merge table is checked against the hand computation, then one line switches the alphabet from characters to UTF-8 bytes and 𠊎 goes from "no id" to four byte tokens | standard library only | anything with Python 3 |
| [Demo 3 · same sums, three ways of writing the numbers](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w02_d3_digits) | p46 | Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen3 8B add random 4-, 7- and 10-digit numbers written plain, with thousands separators, and one digit per token; on Llama the commas lift 10-digit accuracy from 20 % to 84 % while the digit-by-digit Qwen barely moves — and the spaced-digit spelling collapses on both, because neither was trained on it | `mlx` + `mlx-lm`, two 4-bit models (≈ 4.5 GB each) | **Apple silicon only** |

Tested on one machine only — an Apple M5 Max (64 GB, no CUDA), macOS 26.6, Python 3.12 — with the versions pinned in `demos/versions.lock`. "Any laptop" means the code depends on nothing platform-specific, not that it was verified elsewhere. Terminal prompts are in Chinese; Enter advances, `q` quits.

## References
- **JM3** ch 2 *Words and Tokens* (the new chapter title in the 2026-08-19 release, rewritten for exactly this material)
- **RAS** ch 2 (BPE from scratch); **HOLLM** ch 2 *Tokens and Embeddings* (the best visualizations)
- **ZZM** ch 7 *Word Segmentation and Tokenization* — includes a BPE implementation and **Chinese word segmentation**, the only book on our list that treats it. **Note that the code is PaddleNLP: read it, do not run it**
- Sennrich, Haddow & Birch, **Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units**, ACL 2016 — where BPE entered NLP
- Kudo, **Subword Regularization: Improving Neural Network Translation Models with Multiple Subword Candidates**, ACL 2018 — the Unigram LM and sampling over segmentations
- Kudo & Richardson, **SentencePiece: A simple and language independent subword tokenizer and detokenizer for Neural Text Processing**, EMNLP 2018 (system demonstrations)
- Provilkov, Emelianenko & Voita, **BPE-Dropout: Simple and Effective Subword Regularization**, ACL 2020 — the same sampling effect for BPE: randomly skip merges at encoding time
- Rajaraman, Jiao & Ramchandran, **Toward a Theory of Tokenization in LLMs**, arXiv:2404.08335 (NeurIPS 2024; the conference version is titled *An Analysis of Tokenization: Transformers under Markov data*) — a theoretical argument for why tokenization works: on Markov data, a transformer over raw symbols fails to learn higher-order dependence
- Tao et al., **Scaling Laws with Vocabulary: Larger Models Deserve Larger Vocabularies**, NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv:2407.13623) — **this week's main derivation paper**
- Limisiewicz et al., **Compute Optimal Tokenization**, arXiv:2605.01188 (May 2026) — argues that parameter count should scale with data measured in bytes; **a 2026 preprint, and at present the only source for that claim**
- Ali et al., **Tokenizer Choice For LLM Training: Negligible or Crucial?**, arXiv:2310.08754
- Goldman et al., **Unpacking Tokenization: Evaluating Text Compression and its Correlation with Model Performance**, Findings of EMNLP 2024 (arXiv:2403.06265) and Schmidt et al., **Tokenization Is More Than Compression**, EMNLP 2024 (arXiv:2402.18376) — **read as a pair**: the first finds compression correlated with downstream performance, the second minimizes token count outright and does not get a better model
- Singh & Strouse, **Tokenization counts: the impact of tokenization on arithmetic in frontier LLMs**, arXiv:2402.14903 (2024) — right-to-left digit grouping clearly beats left-to-right
- Kaushal & Mahowald, **What do tokens know about their characters and how do they know it?**, NAACL 2022 and Edman, Schmid & Fraser, **CUTE: Measuring LLMs' Understanding of Their Tokens**, EMNLP 2024 — character-level tasks: how much spelling information the model has, and why it still uses it badly
- Land & Bartolo, **Fishing for Magikarp: Automatically Detecting Under-trained Tokens in Large Language Models**, EMNLP 2024 (arXiv:2405.05417) — automatic detection of glitch tokens
- Petrov et al., **Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages**, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2305.15425) — the same content costs very different numbers of tokens across languages, and that becomes cost, latency and usable context
- Liu et al., **SuperBPE: Space Travel for Language Models**, COLM 2025 (arXiv:2503.13423) — superword tokens that cross whitespace; the "bigger tokens" direction after BPE
- Xue et al., **ByT5: Towards a Token-Free Future with Pre-trained Byte-to-Byte Models**, TACL 10:291–306, 2022; Yu et al., **MEGABYTE: Predicting Million-byte Sequences with Multiscale Transformers**, arXiv:2305.07185 (2023); Pagnoni et al., **Byte Latent Transformer: Patches Scale Better Than Tokens**, arXiv:2412.09871; Hwang, Wang & Gu, **Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling**, arXiv:2507.07955 (2025) — four points on the "no tokens" line, from raw bytes to learned dynamic chunking (H-Net)
- Cui, Yang & Yao, **Efficient and Effective Text Encoding for Chinese LLaMA and Alpaca**, arXiv:2304.08177 (2023) — twenty thousand Chinese tokens added to LLaMA's vocabulary, then continued pre-training
- Hsu et al., **Breeze-7B Technical Report**, arXiv:2403.02712 (2024) — an industrial technical report from MediaTek Research, not a peer-reviewed paper; extends Mistral's vocabulary with Traditional Chinese tokens and reports the change in compression and speed. **One of the few public sources with numbers on Traditional Chinese token efficiency**
- Minixhofer, Ponti & Vulić, **Zero-Shot Tokenizer Transfer**, arXiv:2405.07883 (2024) — swapping a model's tokenizer without retraining
- The prompt-boundary problem and token healing: search *token healing*, *prompt boundary problem tokenization*, *language models over characters from tokens*
- Glitch tokens were first reported in a blog post: search *SolidGoldMagikarp*

> **The research gap on Traditional Chinese, Taiwanese and Hakka tokenization**: what exists are numbers measured in passing in individual model reports (the Breeze-7B report above); **there is no systematic comparison of tokenizers on Traditional Chinese, Taiwanese or Hakka**. The related resources are evaluation suites, not tokenizer studies: Chen et al., **TMLU** — *Measuring Taiwanese Mandarin Language Understanding* (arXiv:2403.20180) and Tam et al., **TMMLU+** — *An Improved Traditional Chinese Evaluation Suite for Foundation Model* (arXiv:2403.01858). The comparison table in this week's class is therefore measured live, in the room — which makes it a genuine research opportunity.
